title: Persistence — name the mechanism
description:
Tunde: 'You found the binary. Now tell me how The Griot ensured it ran every time anyone opened a new shell on this box. Don't tell me about cron — there is no cron entry. Don't tell me about systemd — no unit either. The persistence is in plain sight in the evidence you read in task 1.'

Write an analyst note (200+ words) that:

1. **Names the persistence mechanism** in one precise sentence — the file modified, what it does on shell startup, and which user account it piggybacks on. Cite the exact `/evidence/fs/...` path you read.

2. **Quotes the line of evidence** that proves it (the line in `bash_history` where `root` modified the file, AND the `source` line in `.bashrc` itself). Two code-block quotes minimum.

3. **Names the MITRE ATT&CK technique** — the answer is in the `T1546.*` sub-technique family (Event Triggered Execution). Quote the technique ID + full name as MITRE writes it (visit https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/ to verify the sub-technique number).

4. **Explains why this beats a cron-based check.** One paragraph: what would a defender miss if they only audited `crontab -l`, `systemctl list-unit-files`, and `at -l`?

5. **Proposes one detection.** Concrete: a Wazuh syscheck rule, an osquery query against the `file_events` table, a Sigma rule pattern, or a Falco macro. Name the artefact the rule would watch for (mtime change on `~/.bashrc`, syscall pattern, file integrity hash).

6. **One mistake I almost made:** 40+ word section. The seductive wrong answer here is naming `.bash_profile` — explain why this evidence points to `.bashrc` specifically, not `.bash_profile`, and what `bash` actually sources in interactive non-login vs login shells (cite `man bash` §INVOCATION).

**Citation bar:**
- MITRE technique ID + name quoted in full (made-up IDs lose 4 pts each).
- One detection-engineering source (Wazuh, osquery, Sigma, Falco, Atomic Red Team T1546.004) — quote which one and the rule pattern.
- `bash(1)` man page reference (specifically the INVOCATION section that distinguishes login vs interactive shells).

Submission: in-platform (narrative, no tables needed).

---

**Universal grading rule.** Generic answers fail. Every claim in your submission must be tied to specific evidence — an artefact from the lab (file path, log line, command output, payload, screenshot) **and** at least one external citation where research is relevant (NIST section number, MITRE technique ID, CVE, vendor advisory, ISO control ID, GDPR article). Claims without an attached artefact, timestamp, payload, standard section, or business constraint earn zero for that claim. Lab-only answers earn partial credit. External-only answers earn partial credit. Full credit requires both.
